query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the heavy Hf element with additional Nb (i.e. substituting HfMoTaTiZr with a similar equiatomic alloy such as MoNbTaTiZr or Hf‐reduced HfMoNbTaTi) will lower the overall alloy density without compromising its high strength and elevated‐temperature performance up to approximately 1000 °C. This substitution preserves the homogeneous solid-solution microstructure and maintains solid-solution strengthening.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy with a density of about 10.21 g/cm³ and excellent RT yield strength but limited ductility due to the presence of heavy elements.
generation.intervention: Partially or wholly replace Hf with an equivalent amount of Nb to produce a Hf-reduced (or Hf-free) composition such as HfMoNbTaTi (or MoNbTaTiZr) while keeping the overall atomic percentages similar.
generation.conditions: Mechanical performance evaluated at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to roughly 1000 °C under quasi-static loading (tensile/compressive tests).
generation.structural_mediator: The alloy’s solid-solution phase and homogeneous microstructure, with the lighter Nb atoms substituting for a fraction of the heavier Hf atoms to reduce the overall mass density while maintaining solid-solution strengthening.
generation.mechanism: Since Nb is significantly lighter than Hf but still imparts effective solution strengthening and ductility, substituting Hf with Nb is expected to reduce the density. The lighter element contributes to a lower average atomic mass while preserving dislocation–solute interactions and high-temperature stability, thereby maintaining strength and toughness at both room temperature and up to approximately 1000 °C.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit a lower measured density (a substantial reduction from 10.21 g/cm³) while showing comparable yield strength and ductility at room temperature and sufficient strength at elevated temperatures (around 1000 °C) relative to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with high strength at room and elevated temperatures but a relatively high density (~10.21 g/cm³).
generation.boundary: Evaluation will be limited to temperatures from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C and under quasi-static mechanical loading conditions; effects on oxidation resistance or long-term thermal stability are not addressed.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements in density reduction and any minor trade-offs in elevated‐temperature yield strength are uncertain without experimental validation; the balance between strength and ductility may be sensitive to exact compositional adjustments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set of the baseline HfMoTaTiZr alloy and one set of the modified alloy in which Hf is partially (or fully) replaced with Nb (e.g. HfMoNbTaTi or MoNbTaTiZr) using the same casting process followed by identical homogenization. Measure the density, perform room-temperature tensile/compressive tests, and conduct elevated-temperature (e.g. 800 °C and 1000 °C) mechanical tests on both sets.
measurements: Room temperature tensile/compressive yield strength and ductility
Elevated-temperature yield strength and work-hardening behavior at circa 800 °C and 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified (Hf-reduced) alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in density while maintaining mechanical properties (yield strength and ductility) within an acceptable margin of the baseline alloy at room temperature and at approximately 1000 °C, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: There are some researches working on the addition of Al [,], Mo [], Ti [], V [], or Zr [], but few of them focus on the elevated-temperature mechanical performance and the overall effect of the constituent elements. To understand the elemental effect on mechanical properties, equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy is firstly designed as a base alloy by adding the high modulus refractory element Mo to HfNbTaTiZr. Then the subtraction method is used to analyze each elemental effect in the equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr. Thus, in this study, six alloys HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi are investigated and compared on their microstructure. Further, the compressive properties at room temperature and at elevated temperature are investigated. By comparing HfMoNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr, the influence of the addition of Mo can be understood. Likewise, the influence of the addition of Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr can be articulated. In addition, promising compositions were found and further improved design is suggested. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solid solution strengthening effect will be discussed.

The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo.
